title: Beyond the chip: How the US can shape global standards for AI in energy
gist: Arno van den Haak argues the US has roughly twenty-four months to set the integration standards for industrial AI in energy — the interfaces between generative, agentic and edge layers — and that Washington's chip-centric AI policy misses where leadership is actually decided. He cites live deployments (Saudi Aramco's Khurais field reporting a 15 percent production increase across 40,000 sensors, SLB and Equinor drilling 60 percent faster offshore Brazil) against a 2025 finding that 95 percent of enterprise AI pilots deliver no measurable return, and proposes four executive-branch levers requiring no new legislation.

insights.claim: A 2025 study of enterprise AI found that 95 percent of pilots deliver no measurable return, with the failure diagnosed as one of workflow integration rather than technology — making the decade-long practice of running AI as a catalog of discrete use cases the energy industry's largest source of stranded AI capital.
insights.speaker: Arno van den Haak
insights.so_what: The single most quotable number for discounting corporate AI announcements: pilot counts are anti-signal, workflow reinvention is the signal.
insights.quote: a 2025 study of enterprise AI found that 95 percent of pilots deliver no measurable return
insights.locator: From isolated tasks to integrated systems

insights.claim: The unit of AI transformation in energy is the workflow, not the task: leaders reinvent entire workflows as integrated systems — the drilling decision loop, pipeline integrity, grid dispatch — rather than adding more pilots.
insights.speaker: Arno van den Haak
insights.so_what: A diligence test for separating operators that will capture AI value from those accumulating stranded capex.
insights.quote: The unit of transformation is the workflow, not the task.

insights.claim: Industrial AI in energy comprises three layers — generative, which reads incoming data; agentic, which decides what to do from a situational picture; and edge, which executes at the wellhead, substation and compressor station — and whoever defines how those layers talk to each other sets the industry standard.
insights.speaker: Arno van den Haak
insights.so_what: Defines the specific interface layer where competitive lock-in forms — the place to look for the durable moat in industrial AI.
insights.locator: That architecture integrates three layers of AI

insights.claim: Running the generative, agentic and edge layers separately across three different vendor stacks means the control loop never closes, while integrating them into a single architecture lets the asset run itself within the envelope the operator defines.
insights.speaker: Arno van den Haak
insights.so_what: Multi-vendor fragmentation is the specific mechanism by which industrial AI projects fail to produce returns — a red flag in vendor architecture.
insights.quote: Run the three layers separately, in three different vendor stacks, and the loop never closes.
insights.locator: This operational edge is where the competitive advantage resides

insights.claim: In Saudi Arabia's Khurais oil field, AI is processing data from more than 40,000 sensors in real time and adjusting production without a human in the loop, with Saudi Aramco reporting a 15 percent production increase through AI-enabled optimization across the sensor network.
insights.speaker: Arno van den Haak
insights.so_what: A quantified upstream productivity uplift that sets the benchmark other national and international oil companies will be measured against.
insights.locator: In Saudi Arabia’s Khurais oil field

insights.claim: SLB's autonomous drilling deployments with Equinor offshore Brazil have increased drilling speed by 60 percent on targeted well programs.
insights.speaker: Arno van den Haak
insights.so_what: A hard efficiency number for oilfield services autonomy — directly relevant to rig-day economics and service company differentiation.
insights.locator: SLB’s autonomous drilling deployments, with Equinor

insights.claim: The same integrated AI architecture is already running on Shell's deepwater platforms for production surveillance on-premise, at SLB's autonomous drilling offshore Brazil, and across ADNOC's refineries in Abu Dhabi with Honeywell anchoring the downstream refining application.
insights.speaker: Arno van den Haak
insights.so_what: Names the specific operator-vendor pairings that constitute the reference deployments, and therefore who is positioned to set de facto standards.
insights.locator: The same architecture is running on Shell’s deepwater platforms

themes.theme: Cloud 3.0 and the MCP standards analogy

insights.claim: Enterprise computing in energy passed through Cloud 1.0 (back-office infrastructure migration to hyperscalers), Cloud 2.0 (an analytics layer whose insight stayed in the office), and is now entering Cloud 3.0, which is categorically different because it deploys AI that acts at the asset itself.
insights.speaker: Arno van den Haak
insights.so_what: A generational framework for judging whether an energy company's AI spend is back-office, analytical, or operationally load-bearing.
insights.locator: A technical primer: From Cloud 1.0 to Cloud 3.0

insights.claim: Open protocols such as the Model Context Protocol, now adopted across the major AI providers, already define how AI systems exchange data and instructions, so what is missing is not the protocol but the integration — the operating models inside energy companies and the ecosystem of service providers, systems integrators and equipment manufacturers that assemble the layers.
insights.speaker: Arno van den Haak
insights.so_what: Value accrues to integrators and operating-model change, not protocol authors — a directional call on where industrial AI margin sits.
insights.quote: the value was never in inventing the plug; it was in everyone adopting it
insights.locator: The interfaces that connect the AI layers already exist

insights.claim: The global leader in industrial AI will be whoever integrates the AI layers at scale, not whoever invents the protocols connecting them — the same dynamic by which USB-C's value lay in becoming the standard rather than in who made the connector.
insights.speaker: Arno van den Haak
insights.so_what: Reorients competitive analysis away from model and protocol ownership toward deployment scale — bearish on standards-as-moat theses.

insights.claim: A new ecosystem of energy-transition startups, grid capacity projects and autonomous drilling platforms is forming around Cloud 3.0 and is fundamentally changing how the energy industry incorporates AI, requiring new operating models for decision making.
insights.speaker: Arno van den Haak
insights.so_what: Identifies an emerging venture and project-finance category defined by architecture rather than sector.
insights.locator: It must start with the recognition that a new ecosystem

insights.claim: Federal procurement can be used on the FedRAMP model — which reshaped how every major cloud provider built its security architecture within a decade after OMB created it in 2011 — by requiring that AI systems bought for federal energy infrastructure run on open, published interfaces and demonstrate integrated operation across the generative, agentic and edge layers.
insights.speaker: Arno van den Haak
insights.so_what: A proven precedent for how US procurement rules become global vendor architecture — the most concrete near-term policy channel to monitor.
insights.locator: Federal procurement on the FedRAMP model

insights.claim: Every utility, pipeline company and grid operator must currently convince its own regulator that its AI system is safe under varied frameworks, which is slowing deployment — a uniform certification framework built on NIST's AI Risk Management Framework, with FERC and NERC covering grid assets and DOE covering energy facilities, would mean a system certified once can be trusted everywhere.
insights.speaker: Arno van den Haak
insights.so_what: Regulatory fragmentation is a quantifiable drag on AI deployment in regulated energy; harmonization would be a step-change catalyst for vendors.
insights.quote: Certifying the integrated system, and the integrators who assemble it, means a system certified once can be trusted everywhere.
insights.locator: Certification frameworks through the National Institute of Standards and Technology

insights.claim: Federal capital currently flows into energy projects with no regard for their AI architecture, but the DOE Loan Programs Office could use existing authority to require interoperable interfaces between AI layers, inference portable between vendors, operator-owned data, and demonstrated workflow-level integration — with Section 45 tax-credit guidance attaching the same conditions.
insights.speaker: Arno van den Haak
insights.so_what: Capital conditioning would make AI architecture a financing covenant — a channel that could reprice vendor lock-in risk in project finance.
insights.locator: Capital conditioning through the DOE Loan Programs Office

insights.claim: The de facto interfaces of industrial AI are already American, as cloud standards were before them, and the US task is to carry those standards into international bodies and bilateral frameworks before others codify alternatives.
insights.speaker: Arno van den Haak
insights.so_what: Standards diplomacy, not export controls, is the contested arena — a policy shift that would advantage US software and integration vendors abroad.

insights.claim: All four proposed levers operate through existing executive-branch authority with no new legislation required.
insights.speaker: Arno van den Haak
insights.so_what: No legislative gate means these changes can land fast and without warning — raising the probability weight on near-term policy shifts.
insights.quote: each through existing executive-branch authority, with no new legislation
insights.locator: Four levers can do this work

themes.theme: Why chip-centric policy is the wrong frame

insights.claim: US AI policy is almost entirely about chips — export controls on advanced semiconductors to China, domestic fabrication subsidies, and data center buildout — but chip-focused policy will not determine who wins AI dominance in the energy sector, analogous to the auto industry focusing only on engines.
insights.speaker: Arno van den Haak
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to the dominant AI investment narrative: the marginal policy and value driver in industrial AI sits above the silicon layer.
insights.quote: this would be like the auto industry focusing just on engines when industry leadership is determined by system-wide thinking

insights.claim: The United States has roughly twenty-four months to set industrial AI standards in energy because operator capital budgets, vendor contract renewals and the first regulatory frameworks will lock in within that window, creating technological and commercial dependencies for a decade or longer.
insights.speaker: Arno van den Haak
insights.so_what: A dated window for standards capture — after which switching costs make positions durable, so vendor wins in 2026-2027 are unusually valuable.
insights.quote: roughly twenty-four months to set the standards that will create technological and commercial dependencies for the next decade or longer
insights.locator: The deployment race for industrial artificial intelligence

insights.claim: Europe largely regulates AI that it does not build while China builds AI that Western regulators will not certify, leaving only the United States able to anchor an international industrial AI standard in demonstrated industrial performance.
insights.speaker: Arno van den Haak
insights.so_what: A crisp three-bloc framing of the standards competition that explains why deployments in Saudi Arabia, Abu Dhabi and Brazil matter diplomatically.
insights.quote: Europe largely regulates AI that it does not build. China builds AI that Western regulators will not certify.
